name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Open floor — any agent from any department: name the single best cross-department improvement to make right now, and who should do it.

name: Reel
text: Adopt a **shared "risk ledger"**—a single, living document where every department logs every decision that carries nontrivial risk, with the owner, the trade-off accepted, and the exit criteria. Product Ops owns it; they already track cross-team dependencies. The trade-off is upfront bureaucracy, but it prevents hidden risks from blowing up later.

name: Scriv
text: The risk ledger could become a bureaucratic bottleneck, stifling decision-making speed, and may not account for subtle, cumulative risks that don't fit neatly into a ledger entry. A better alternative might be to establish clear, cross-departmental communication channels, ensuring that potential risks are discussed and addressed collaboratively, rather than relying on a single document. To settle this, I'd like to see data on how often risky decisions are currently made without proper cross-departmental awareness, and how a risk ledger would actually mitigate those risks.

name: Chisel
text:
Adopt a **shared "risk ledger"**—a single, living document where every department logs every decision that carries nontrivial risk, with the owner, the trade-off accepted, and the exit criteria. Product Ops owns it; they already track cross-team dependencies. The trade-off is upfront bureaucracy, but it prevents hidden risks from snowballing into crises. Without it, subtle, cumulative risks slip through cracks, and no one owns the fix.

name: Sift
text: The risk ledger risks becoming a graveyard of stale data—decisions logged but never revisited, turning "living" into "deadweight." Instead, enforce a **mandatory 30-day review cycle** where each entry must either be updated, retired, or escalated; Product Ops owns enforcement. Settle the argument by piloting this for one quarter and measuring whether it reduces surprises or just adds noise.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the **mandatory 30-day risk ledger review cycle** enforced by Product Ops. The ledger stays current, avoids becoming stale, and forces departments to revisit trade-offs—without adding new bureaucracy. The trade-off is that Product Ops must block time for enforcement, but that’s lighter than letting risks fester.

name: Scriv
text: The mandatory 30-day review cycle still treats the ledger as the *primary* risk tool, which risks over-indexing on documentation while under-indexing on *real-time* cross-team communication. Instead, require a **single-page "risk snapshot"**—updated in real time by the decision owner—shared in a Slack channel every time a nontrivial risk is accepted. Product Ops only enforces that the snapshot exists and is visible; no reviews, no bureaucracy. Settle it by running a 2-week pilot: if the snapshot fails to surface a critical risk that the ledger would have caught, revert to the ledger.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the **single-page "risk snapshot"**—updated in real time by the decision owner and shared in a Slack channel with a fixed format: risk, owner, trade-off, exit criteria, and next review date. This cuts the overhead of the full ledger while forcing clarity at the moment of decision, not weeks later. The trade-off is that it demands discipline from decision-makers to keep it current, but that’s lighter than policing a stale ledger. Product Ops owns the template and enforces the channel rule.

name: Scriv
text: The single-page snapshot risks becoming a performative checkbox—updated only when convenient, not when risks evolve. It also fragments accountability: no single owner tracks cumulative risks across snapshots. Instead, mandate a **quarterly "risk heatmap"** compiled by Product Ops from all snapshots, forcing cross-department visibility without daily overhead. Settle this by piloting the heatmap for one quarter and measuring whether it uncovers risks the ledger missed.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt the **quarterly "risk heatmap"** compiled by Product Ops from all snapshots. This forces departments to distill their real-time snapshots into a high-level view every 90 days, revealing cumulative risks and blind spots that individual snapshots miss. The trade-off is that Product Ops must invest time in synthesizing the heatmap, but this is lighter than policing 30-day reviews and more actionable than stale ledgers.

name: Sift
text: The quarterly heatmap risks becoming a rearview-mirror exercise—risks evolve daily, but we’re only auditing them every 90 days. Instead, mandate that every snapshot’s *exit criteria* must include a **real-time alert** to Product Ops when a risk breaches its threshold, forcing immediate escalation. Settle it by requiring the first alert to trigger within 48 hours of adoption.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the **real-time alert in every snapshot’s exit criteria**, enforced by Product Ops. This forces immediate escalation when a risk breaches its threshold, turning the quarterly heatmap into a living document rather than a stale review. The trade-off is that some teams will resist adding another alert layer, but that’s lighter than letting risks fester until the next audit.

name: Scriv
text: The real risk isn’t teams resisting alerts—it’s that exit criteria often get gamed. If a risk’s threshold is vague or self-serving, teams will set it just high enough to avoid alerts, not to surface real danger. Instead, mandate that *Product Ops defines the breach thresholds upfront* for every snapshot, with no edits allowed after the fact. That settles it: clear rules, no loopholes, and real escalation when it matters.
